entities.name: Stefanos Gabrielopoulos
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Stefanos Gabrielopoulos (died c. 1333) was a formidable magnate and semi-independent ruler who carved out a significant domain in western Thessaly during the tumultuous early 14th century. Operating amidst the protracted Byzantine civil war of 1321–1328 and the subsequent weakening of imperial authority, Gabrielopoulos leveraged his local power base and military strength to establish de facto autonomy. His strategic importance lay in his ability to control a vital, fertile region on the periphery of the shrinking Byzantine Empire, making him a crucial, if often opportunistic, player in the fragmented political landscape of the southern Balkans.

Initially asserting his independence, Gabrielopoulos eventually sought formal recognition from the Byzantine Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, pledging nominal allegiance in exchange for imperial legitimacy. This diplomatic maneuvering led to his investiture with the prestigious court title of *sebastokrator*, a high honor typically reserved for members of the imperial family or close associates, around 1330. This title granted him significant prestige and a measure of legal authority within the Byzantine system, consolidating his rule over cities like Trikala and the surrounding agricultural lands. His reign represented a common pattern of regional decentralization and the rise of local strongmen during the Palaiologan era, as the central government struggled to maintain control over its dwindling territories.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Stefanos Gabrielopoulos's brief, independent rule in Thessaly exemplifies the fragmentation of the late Byzantine Empire, and his death directly enabled the expansion of the Serbian Empire into a strategically vital region, reshaping the political map of the Balkans.
